title: Pronoun case, agreement and clear reference
blurb: Choose I or me, who or whom, and the right pronoun for every antecedent, and fix pronouns that point nowhere or in two directions.
question: A nursing applicant writes, “My mentor and me volunteered at the shelter, and she later wrote a reference for Dr. Lin and myself.” How many pronoun errors are there, and how would you fix each one?

teach.body: Formally, a pronoun replaces a noun, called its antecedent, and must be in the correct case (subjective, objective or possessive), agree with its antecedent in number and person, and refer clearly to one antecedent. Plain English: pick the form that fits the pronoun's job in the sentence, make it match the word it replaces, and make sure the reader knows exactly which word that is. The TEAS tests all three: case, agreement and clear reference.

head: Subjective (does)
Objective (receives)
Possessive (owns)
teach.caption: Subjective for subjects (and after linking verbs in formal writing: “It is I”). Objective for objects of verbs and of prepositions (to, for, with, between). Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe.

steps.label: Put the pair back
steps.sub: Ana and I went. For Ana and me.

teach.caption: The same test fixes “we/us + noun”: drop the noun. “(We) nurses agree.” “for (us) nurses.”
Use myself only when I is already the subject (“I reminded myself”) or for emphasis.

teach.h: Who vs whom: the he/him test
teach.body: Who is subjective, like he. Whom is objective, like him. Answer the question or rearrange the clause, then substitute. “___ is calling?” He is calling, so who. “___ did you call?” You called him, so whom. “The aide ___ we hired starts Monday”: we hired him, so whom. Whoever and whomever work the same way: the job inside its own clause decides, so “Send the form to whoever needs it” (whoever needs).

A pronoun matches its antecedent. Plural antecedent, plural pronoun: “The nurses renewed their licenses.” A thing takes it or its: “The clinic posted its hours.” Keep the person steady too: shifting from one or a person (third person) to you (second person) is an error. “If a person studies daily, you will pass” should be “If students study daily, they will pass.”

teach.h: Two ways a reference goes wrong

children.label: Ambiguous
children.sub: When Maya called Rosa, she was upset.

children.label: Vague
children.sub: In the article, they say sleep helps.

teach.caption: Fix both by naming the noun: “Maya was upset when she called Rosa.” “The article's authors say sleep helps.”

teach.h: Scenario: Marcus fixes his personal statement
teach.body: Nursing applicant Marcus Reed drafts: “My mentor and me volunteered at the shelter, and she later wrote a reference for Dr. Lin and myself.” Drop test 1: “me volunteered” fails, so “My mentor and I.” Drop test 2: “a reference for myself” fails because myself has no I to point back to, so “for Dr. Lin and me.” The she is clear: the mentor is the only antecedent before it that fits. Two errors, two fixes.

teach.text: “Between you and I” sounds polite but is wrong: between is a preposition, so both pronouns are objective (between you and me). The reverse trap is “whom” used as a subject because it sounds formal: “the nurse whom answered” should be “the nurse who answered.”

items: Subjective (I, we, he, she, they, who) for subjects; objective (me, us, him, her, them, whom) for objects and after prepositions.
Use the drop test for pairs: cover the other noun and read the pronoun alone.
Who = he (subject); whom = him (object). Decide inside the pronoun's own clause.
Myself only reflects an I already in the sentence or adds emphasis.
Pronouns agree with antecedents in number and person; no shift from one to you.
Every pronoun needs one clear antecedent: fix ambiguous she and vague they by naming the noun.

summary: You can now choose the right pronoun case with the drop test and the he/him test, and keep pronouns in agreement with their antecedents. You can also spot ambiguous and vague references and rewrite them so the reader knows exactly who is meant.

A.q: Which pronoun correctly completes the sentence? “The charge nurse asked Kiara and ___ to restock the supply room.”
options: I
myself
me
she
A.why: Kiara and ___ is the object of asked, so the objective case is needed. Drop test: “asked me,” so “asked Kiara and me.”

whyNot.0: I is subjective; “asked I” fails the drop test.
whyNot.1: Myself is reflexive and needs an I earlier in the sentence; there is none.
whyNot.3: She is subjective; as an object of asked it would have to be her.

A.q: Which sentence uses who or whom correctly?
options: Whom is covering the night shift tonight?
To who should I send the incident report?
The nurse whom answered was very kind.
The patient whom we called is here now.
A.why: Inside the clause, “we called him,” so the objective whom is correct.

whyNot.0: The pronoun is the subject of is covering (he is covering), so it should be Who.
whyNot.1: After the preposition to, the objective whom is needed: “To whom should I send...”
whyNot.2: The pronoun is the subject of answered (he answered), so it should be who.

A.q: Which sentence shows correct pronoun-antecedent agreement?
options: The volunteers brought their own lunches to the drive.
Applicants should bring his or her ID to the test site.
When a patient arrives, you should check in at the desk.
The nursing students left her backpacks in the lounge.
A.why: Volunteers is plural, so the plural their agrees with it.

whyNot.1: Applicants is plural, so the pronoun should be their, not the singular his or her.
whyNot.2: The sentence shifts from third person (a patient) to second person (you).
whyNot.3: Students is plural, so her (singular) does not agree; it should be their.

B.q: Which sentence uses the pronoun correctly?
options: Please send the schedule to Dr. Patel or myself.
Dr. Patel and myself will review the schedule.
I reminded myself to review the schedule.
The schedule was reviewed by Dr. Patel and I.
B.why: Myself correctly reflects the subject I in the same sentence.

whyNot.0: There is no I for myself to reflect; the object of to should be me.
whyNot.1: Myself cannot be a subject; it should be “Dr. Patel and I.”
whyNot.3: After the preposition by, the objective me is needed: “by Dr. Patel and me.”

B.q: Which pair of pronouns correctly completes the sentence? “___ nursing applicants were told to arrive by 7:30 a.m., so the proctor checked IDs for ___ first.”
options: Us / we
We / us
Us / us
We / we
B.why: Drop the noun: “We were told” (subject, so we) and “for us” (object of a preposition, so us).

whyNot.0: Both are reversed: “Us were told” and “for we” both fail the drop test.
whyNot.2: “Us were told” fails: the subject needs we.
whyNot.3: “For we” fails: the object of for needs us.

B.q: Which sentence has a clear pronoun reference?
options: After Rosa met Maya at the library, she felt calmer.
Rosa was upset about the exam when she called Maya.
On the news, they said the clinic will expand soon.
Tom told Jaden that his badge had expired today.
B.why: She can only be Rosa, because she is the one who called Maya.

whyNot.0: She could be Rosa or Maya, so the reference is ambiguous.
whyNot.2: They has no antecedent; name the source (the reporter, the hospital).
whyNot.3: His could mean Tom's badge or Jaden's badge, so the reference is ambiguous.

C.q: Which revision corrects every pronoun error in this sentence? “Between you and I, Jordan and me were nervous before the exam.”
options: Between you and me, Jordan and I were nervous
Between you and I, Jordan and I were nervous
Between you and me, Jordan and me were nervous
Between you and myself, Jordan and I were nervous
C.why: Between is a preposition, so me (objective). “Jordan and ___ were nervous” is a subject, so I (subjective).

whyNot.1: Fixes the subject but leaves “between you and I,” which needs the objective me.
whyNot.2: Fixes the preposition but leaves “Jordan and me were,” which needs the subjective I.
whyNot.3: Myself has no I to reflect; after between, use me.

C.q: Which pronoun correctly completes the sentence? “Give the extra parking pass to ___ arrives first tomorrow.”
options: whomever
whom
whoever
who's
C.why: The pronoun is the subject of arrives inside its own clause (he arrives), so the subjective whoever is correct. The whole clause is the object of to.

whyNot.0: Whomever is objective, but the pronoun is the subject of arrives. The preposition to does not decide the case here.
whyNot.1: Whom is objective and cannot be the subject of arrives.
whyNot.3: Who's means who is: “to who is arrives” makes no sense.

C.q: Which sentence avoids a shift in person?
options: When one arrives late, you lose the chance to test.
When students arrive late, you lose the chance to test.
When a student arrives late, we lose the chance to test.
When students arrive late, they lose the chance to test.
C.why: Students (third person plural) is matched by they (third person plural), so person and number stay consistent.

whyNot.0: Shifts from one (third person) to you (second person).
whyNot.1: Shifts from students (third person) to you (second person).
whyNot.2: Shifts from a student (third person) to we (first person).

reteach.title: Pronouns are name tags
reteach.question: Think of a pronoun as a name tag that stands in for a person. What has to be true about the tag for everyone in the room to know who it means?

blocks.h: The right tag, worn the right way
blocks.body: A name tag must fit the role: a doer wears the subject tag (I, he, she, we, they, who), and a receiver wears the object tag (me, him, her, us, them, whom). The tag must match the person: one person, a singular tag; a group, a plural tag. And it must point to one person only: if two people in the room could be “she,” the tag has failed and you need to write the name.

blocks.text: Fancy is not the same as correct. Myself and whom sound formal, but they are wrong when the sentence needs me or who.

explain.body: Subjects take I, we, he, she, they. Objects of verbs and prepositions take me, us, him, her, them. With a pair, drop the other noun and read the pronoun alone.

test.q: Which pronoun correctly completes the sentence? “Ms. Vega and ___ will proctor the anatomy exam on Friday.”
options: me
I
myself
her
test.why: The pair is the subject of will proctor. Drop test: “I will proctor,” so “Ms. Vega and I.”

whyNot.0: “Me will proctor” fails: me is objective.
whyNot.2: Myself needs an I earlier in the sentence to reflect.
whyNot.3: “Her will proctor” fails: her is objective; the subject form is she.

explain.body: Rewrite the clause as a statement and swap in he or him. He means who; him means whom. Only the pronoun's job inside its own clause matters.

test.q: Which word correctly completes the question? “___ is responsible for the supply order this week?”
options: Who
Whom
Whose
Whomever
test.why: The pronoun is the subject of is responsible (he is responsible), so the subjective who is correct.

whyNot.1: Whom is objective (him) and cannot be the subject of is.
whyNot.2: Whose shows possession and would need a noun after it (whose team).
whyNot.3: Whomever is objective and is not used to begin a direct question.

explain.body: Singular antecedents take singular pronouns; plural take plural. Things take it and its. Keep the same person throughout: one ... one, students ... they, you ... you.

test.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “Each of the clinics must post ___ weekend hours on the front door.”
options: his or her
it's
they're
its
test.why: Each is singular, and a clinic is a thing, so the singular possessive its is correct.

whyNot.0: His or her refers to people; a clinic is a thing, so the pronoun is its.
whyNot.1: It's means it is: “post it is weekend hours” makes no sense.
whyNot.2: They're means they are, which is not a possessive.

explain.body: A pronoun must point to exactly one antecedent. If two nouns could fit, or none appears, replace the pronoun with the noun or restructure the sentence.

test.q: Which revision fixes the unclear pronoun in “After the nurse spoke with the patient, she went home”?
options: After speaking with the patient, the nurse went home.
After the nurse spoke with the patient, they went home.
After the nurse spoke with the patient, she then went home.
After the nurse spoke with the patient, her shift ended.
test.why: Naming the nurse as the subject removes the doubt about who went home.

whyNot.1: They is still ambiguous: it could mean the nurse, the patient or both.
whyNot.2: Adding then does nothing to show whether she is the nurse or the patient.
whyNot.3: Her could still be the nurse or the patient, so the reference stays ambiguous.
